items.text: SEASON 11 · EPISODE 3 · DRAFT · CASE-057  The Brennock County EOC radio room · Maya, Fitz (radio systems manager), Quino (dispatch liaison) and Director Oduya · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Six agencies share one room. In the first crest, two of them couldn’t hear each other — and one receiver on the roof has been slowly going deaf.  ⚑ RV-182: radios, licences and the mast are Fitz’s; talkgroups are the agencies’; nobody climbs. RV-186: frequencies illustrative, not assignments. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Radio Interop
items.stakes: Fire and public works couldn't hear each other in the first crest, and fire dispatch's receiver is going deaf.
items.clock: Before the next crest, in 36 hours.
items.reward: Agencies that hear each other on a plan — and a receiver that hears everyone.

objectives.text: Decide how to find the hiss
Decide what happens to the loaner
Decide where the patch plan lives

items.rumor: Interoperability is a plan, not a patch.

items.alt: The radio room: three console positions, the gateway rack and a window onto the antenna mast; Fitz, the radio systems manager, a handheld on his belt, points at fire dispatch's console.

bubbles.text: Nobody's on fire's frequency, and it's hissing like a kettle.
Then something is making it. What's on your mast?

items.caption: Six agencies, one roof.

lines.text: Nobody's on fire's frequency, and it's hissing like a kettle.
Then something is making it. Let's find out what's on your mast.

items.prompt: 09:10. Fire dispatch's receiver hisses; the patch failed last night. How do you find the hiss?
items.risk: Fire dispatch missing a crew's weak call in the next crest.
timeout: Fire dispatch keeps listening through the hiss.

hints.text: What changed on the mast — and what do two transmitters make together?

options.label: Swap fire dispatch's radio for a spare
options.consequence: Changes the victim, not the cause.

options.label: With Fitz, listen to fire's receiver with each transmitter on the mast keyed and unkeyed; then work out what they make together
options.result: Hiss only when the EMS repeater and the loaner are both keyed. 2 × 155.340 − 154.980 = 155.700 — fire's receive.
options.consequence: Evidence on the owner's system, then the arithmetic.

options.label: Turn fire's receiver squelch up until the hiss stops
options.result: The hiss stops — and so do the weak calls from crews in the valley.

options.label: Go up the mast and look at the antennas
options.consequence: Work at height, on someone else's licence.
options.fail: Nobody climbs; the mast is the radio systems manager's, with certified crews.

items.title: A frequency nobody transmitted.
items.body: The hiss comes only when two transmitters on the mast are keyed at once: the EMS repeater on 155.340 MHz and public works' loaner on 154.980, put up last month for the flood. Where strong signals meet something non-linear, they mix. Twice one, minus the other: 155.700 MHz — exactly where fire dispatch listens. Nobody is transmitting on fire's frequency. The mast is.
items.label: Test: find the product — and what fire hears.

items.caption: A signal nobody sent.

items.title: ‘TEMP: PW loaner, 154.980’
items.body: The mast's equipment list, updated in pencil last month: ‘TEMP — Public Works loaner repeater, 154.980 MHz.’ Nobody had run the intermod check that every other entry on the list had been through.

items.prompt: The loaner's intermod lands on fire's receive. What happens to the loaner?
unknown: Another site the loaner can use
items.risk: Fire deaf in the next crest — or public works without its repeater.
timeout: The hiss stays through the next crest.

hints.text: Whose transmitter is it — and what else could it share a mast with?

options.label: Switch the loaner off
options.result: The hiss stops — and public works loses the repeater it needs in the flood.
options.consequence: Fixes fire by breaking public works.

options.label: Fitz moves the loaner to the water-tower site under the county's licence — a certified crew fits it in calm weather — and checks the mast for any other product on a receive frequency
options.result: Tuesday, calm and dry, the crew moves it. The hiss is gone; nothing else lands on a receive frequency.
options.consequence: The owner's transmitter, moved by the owner's people, checked.

options.label: Ask public works to use the loaner only when fire isn't busy
options.consequence: A rule nobody can keep in an activation.

options.label: Reprogram the loaner to a nearby frequency yourself
options.result: Quino: “That's their radio and Fitz's licence.”
options.fail: Frequencies and licences are the radio systems manager's.

items.title: Three letters every ship could read
items.body: In 1906 the nations at the International Radiotelegraph Convention in Berlin agreed a single distress call for every ship at sea, whatever its flag or its equipment: three dots, three dashes, three dots — SOS. It came into force in 1908. The radios were never the hard part. Agreeing, in writing, what they would all say was.

items.text: Act II — “The patch in one person's head”

items.title: The patch in one person's head.
items.body: Maya reads the gateway's patch against each agency's current talkgroups. It joins fire to WORKS-1 — a talkgroup public works retired in the spring when its radios were reprogrammed. Quino goes quiet. The flood patch lived with Marguerite, a dispatcher who retired in April; the binder on the shelf is four years old. Nobody wrote down what she knew because nobody needed to, until last night.
items.label: Test: how long was the plan wrong — and who agrees the fix?

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #104 · AVERY'S LENS  Interoperability is a plan, not a patch  Agencies hear each other because a written plan says which channels join, who runs them and how they're tested — and because every transmitter on a shared mast has been checked for what it makes together.  Two repeaters on one mast manufactured a signal on fire dispatch's frequency, and the flood patch lived in the head of a dispatcher who had retired.

items.alt: The radio room; Quino holds an old binder open at a page of patch settings; Maya reads the gateway screen.

bubbles.text: Marguerite could set that patch up in her sleep. We never wrote it down because we had her.
Then we write it now — with her name on the first page.

items.prompt: Marguerite could set that patch up in her sleep. We never wrote it down because we had her.

options.label: “Then the plan's the thank-you — write down what she knew, with her name on the first page.”
options.reply: She'd like that. She'd also correct it in red pen.

options.label: “That's how knowledge gets lost.”
options.reply: I know how it gets lost. I watched it retire.

options.label: “Can we call her?”
options.reply: We can. Once. Then we write it down.

items.prompt: The flood patch lived in one person's head. Where does it live now?
unknown: Which talkgroups each agency wants joined
items.risk: The next patch failing the same way.
timeout: The gateway is fixed and the binder stays four years old.

hints.text: Who owns each talkgroup — and who decides which ones join?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S11E03). Option B needs Documentation at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Fix the gateway's patch and move on
options.result: It works — until the next reprogramming.
options.consequence: The same patch, still in nobody's binder.

options.label: The agencies agree a written flood patch plan — named talkgroups, net control on the county desk, a weekly test — signed by the director and each agency, printed in the radio room and put in the EOC plan
options.result: Signed Monday. First Tuesday test: fire hears public works, one voice runs it.
options.consequence: A plan the owners wrote, signed and test.

options.label: Fitz updates the old binder himself
options.result: Revision 5, in Fitz's handwriting — and nobody from the agencies has seen it.
options.consequence: The best you can do without the plan process — written, but not agreed.

options.label: Ask Marguerite to come back on call during floods
options.result: She says yes, once. She's seventy-one.
options.consequence: The same single point of failure, borrowed back.

items.alt: A flood patch plan, revision 5: the patch joining fire, public works and EMS through the gateway; net control at the county dispatch desk, named each operational period; started on the director's word; talkgroup names confirmed by each agency quarterly; a test every Tuesday at 10:00; signed by the director, the radio systems manager and each agency.
items.caption: A plan, not a patch.

items.title: rev 4 · ‘WORKS-1’
items.body: The flood patch binder, revision 4, four years old: ‘Patch FIRE-OPS 2 to WORKS-1.’ Public works retired WORKS-1 in the spring and moved to WORKS-FLOOD. The binder never heard.

bubbles.text: The agency's warning said ‘move to higher ground now’. I posted ‘flooding possible, stay alert’.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Agencies hear each other because of a written plan — which talkgroups join, who is net control, how it’s tested — not because of a patch in someone’s head. Transmitters sharing a mast make new frequencies (f = 2f₁ − f₂); a product on a receive frequency is desense. Radios, licences and the mast are the radio systems manager’s, with certified crews for any climbing; talkgroups are the agencies’.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What do you rely on that lives in one person’s head?
